To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the power and time models we derived from measurements of large, scientific, parallel applications accurately predict the performance and energy consumption of these applications.

(i) the power and energy of large, parallel scientific applications can be modeled as a function of CPU frequency; (ii) for a given application, the power and energy are highly sensitive to the frequency; (iii) for a given system, the average frequency sensitivity is application-dependent; (iv) the frequency sensitivity of a given application can vary widely across different supercomputers; (v) the frequency sensitivity can vary widely across applications within a given supercomputer; and (vi) a
the frequency of a processor has a significant impact on the power, time, and energy of scientific applications.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the relationship between CPU frequency and application performance, energy consumption, and power dissipation.
how energy and power properties of supercomputers impact the performance of the scientific applications they are designed to support.
how the energy efficiency of supercomputers will evolve over time and what impact this will have on the performance and cost of running scientific applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the energy consumption of supercomputers can be accurately and reliably predicted and that the energy consumption is dominated by the application workload.
the energy consumption of a supercomputer is not only a function of its size and architecture but also of the applications it runs and their frequency-sensitivity.

we have demonstrated that it is possible to accurately model the energy and power behavior of large-scale parallel scientific applications, and that these models can be used to make predictions that will help guide the design of the future generation of supercomputers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the context of supercomputers, we can accurately model and predict how changes in frequency will impact power and energy.
the models we derive accurately predict application performance, power, energy, EDP and ED2P.
the energy efficiency of a large-scale system is a function of the energy efficiency of its applications.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while there is a great deal of variability in the frequency sensitivity of different applications, most applications exhibit a relatively small frequency sensitivity.

energy modeling is an essential tool for understanding the power and energy behavior of scientific applications, and it enables the development of more accurate and efficient power management techniques for supercomputers.

energy modeling of scientific applications is a powerful tool for understanding the energy behavior of supercomputers, predicting how changes in hardware will impact applications, and determining the best frequency for running applications on a given system.
